 She Opens a High-Yield Savings Account Paying 4.2% to Build a Cushion. Crossing the $2,000 Resource Limit Can Stop Her SSI Check
 Gerelyn Terzo 2026년 11월 5일 목 오전 10:32 UTC 0 Portra / Getty Images (Portra / Getty Images) Quick Read
 SSI recipients lose their entire $994 monthly check if countable savings exceed $2,000 on the 1st of any month, even by $5.
 Interest earned on savings accounts is excluded from SSI income but becomes a countable resource the following month, potentially triggering disqualification.
 ABLE accounts let eligible disabled individuals save up to $100,000 outside the $2,000 resource limit, making them the most powerful savings tool available.
 Americans who work with a financial advisor have saved more than twice as much for retirement, on average. Find out what one could change for you: SmartAsset's free quiz matches you with up to three vetted fiduciary advisors in about five minutes. (Sponsor)
 A woman living on Supplemental Security Income (SSI) opens a high-yield savings account paying 4.2% so a dental bill or car repair won't wipe her out. It's a reasonable move. If her countable savings sit even a few dollars above $2,000 when a month begins, she can lose that entire month's SSI check. The interest doesn't even count as income.
 A lot of money rides on this. In 2026 the federal SSI payment for one person is $994 a month. The confusion is understandable. SSI treats money in a savings account differently from the interest it earns, and that distinction can cost someone an entire monthly payment. It also matters more now that a 4.2% yield beats the 1.8% national average on a 12-month CD by a wide margin.
 Your Balance on the 1st Decides the Whole Month's Check
 The limit on countable resources is $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple. The limit didn't change from 2025 to 2026, even as monthly payments rose by 2.8%. Retirees and people with disabilities can receive bigger checks, but the amount of countable savings they're allowed to keep hasn't budged.
 ------
 Can You Answer These Three Questions? 
 Americans say they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably. Whether that number fits your life depends on three questions most people never work through:
 1. How much can you withdraw each year without running out?
 2. When should you claim Social Security?
 3. How much will taxes take from your 401(k) or IRA?

 Timing is the key detail. The value of your countable resources is what Social Security reviews at the beginning of the month. If you're over the limit at that moment, you can't receive SSI for that month. Going over by a few dollars costs you the whole payment. Being $5 over on November 1 wipes out a $994 check.
 Interest Doesn't Count as SSI Income Today, but It Can Count as a Resource Next Month
 For SSI benefits paid since July 1, 2004, interest earned on a countable resource like a savings account is excluded from income. On a balance of $1,900, a year of interest at 4.2% comes to about $80, and none of it cuts her monthly check.
 Interest left in the account can count toward the $2,000 resource limit the following month. Suppose she has $1,995 saved at the end of October. A month's interest adds roughly $7, which puts her over $2,000 on November 1. In that case about $7 of interest costs her a $994 check, and any part of last month's SSI payment still sitting in checking also counts toward the total.
 What Stays Off the Scale, and What You Must Report
 Plenty of what she has doesn't count at all. Social Security excludes:
 The home she lives in and the land it sits on, whatever it's worth, so paying down or fixing the house doesn't threaten eligibility.
 One vehicle, regardless of value, as long as she or someone in her household uses it for transportation.
 Household goods and personal effects, such as furniture and wedding rings, which means a needed purchase can sometimes do more good than having cash pile up.
 Up to $1,500 in burial funds for her and her spouse individually, although certain life insurance policies and other burial arrangements can reduce that exclusion.
 Up to $100,000 in an Achieving a Better Life Experience account, a state-run savings account for people with disabilities. If her disability began early enough to qualify, this is the most powerful way to build a real cushion.
 Reporting is the other half. Opening a new account counts as a change in resources, and so does a change in an account's value. Report it no later than 10 days after the end of the month in which it happened. Reporting late can bring a penalty of $25 to $100 each time. If checks kept coming while she was over the limit, she'll likely have to pay them back.
 Run the Numbers Before Money Moves
 Add up every countable dollar at month's end. Before moving cash into a new high-yield account, count checking, the new savings account, cash at home and anything left from this month's check. Leave a buffer of a couple hundred dollars under $2,000 so interest and timing quirks can't push you over. When savings run high, spend on excluded items like a car repair or household needs, or move money into an excluded account, before the 1st coming.
 An overpayment notice months later can be difficult to resolve, especially if the money has already been spent. A five-minute balance check at the end of each month can help prevent that surprise. Exclusions, couple rules and state supplements vary. A quick call to Social Security before a big transfer is worth the hold time, since they differ by household.

 The title "financial advisor" isn't legally protected, and plenty of people who use it are paid on commission for the products they sell. A fiduciary is different: they are legally obligated to act in your best interest .
